gloss_terse: Eladah, personal name meaning 'God has adorned'; an Ephraimite ancestor mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:20
gloss_readable: Eladah appears once in the genealogies of Ephraim as a descendant in the tribal lineage. The name combines the divine element 'El' (God) with a verb related to adornment or decoration, suggesting the meaning 'God has adorned.' Like many names in Chronicles' genealogies, it preserves the memory of an Ephraimite clan head whose lineage contributed to the tribe's historical identity.

senses.1: This personal name occurs only in the Chronicler's genealogical record of Ephraim's descendants (1 Chr 7:20). The multilingual evidence shows translators handling it as a proper name, with most preserving the Hebrew form or transliterating it directly. The name's theophoric element 'El' connects it to the broader pattern of Israelite names expressing divine attributes or actions.

gloss_terse: Eluzai, personal name meaning 'God is my strength'; one of David's warriors who joined him at Ziklag
gloss_readable: Eluzai was one of the Benjamite warriors who defected to David during his time at Ziklag, before Saul's death. The name means 'God is my strength,' combining the divine name 'El' with a root related to strength or refuge. This warrior appears in the list of mighty men who came to David's aid when he was still fleeing from Saul, demonstrating the growing support for David's kingship even from Saul's own tribe.

senses.1: This personal name appears only in 1 Chronicles 12:5 (English v. 6) among the Benjamite warriors who joined David at Ziklag. The name's meaning 'God is my strength' reflects the common pattern of theophoric names expressing trust in divine protection. Translation evidence shows consistent treatment as a personal name, with most languages transliterating the Hebrew form.

gloss_terse: Bringing forth thousands, multiplying abundantly; Hiphil participle describing flocks producing offspring in great numbers
gloss_readable: This rare form appears in Psalm 144:13, describing the ideal blessing of agricultural abundance where flocks multiply by thousands. The participle form suggests ongoing, productive fertility—sheep bearing lambs in such numbers that they can be counted in thousands rather than individual animals. This imagery of multiplying flocks represents divine blessing on the land and livestock, a sign of God's favor in an agrarian society.

senses.1: The Hiphil participle occurs only in Psalm 144:13, part of a prayer for national prosperity and blessing. The Spanish 'multiplicados por miles' and French 'multiplier' capture the sense of abundant reproduction. This agricultural imagery describes flocks producing offspring in vast numbers, a concrete sign of God's blessing on the land. The context lists various forms of abundance—full barns, multiplying livestock, absence of warfare—as marks of divine favor.

gloss_terse: Ha-Eleph, place name; a town in the territory of Benjamin, possibly the site of modern Lifta northwest of Jerusalem
gloss_readable: Ha-Eleph was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin in the division of the land. The definite article 'ha' before the name suggests it may have been known as 'the thousand' or possibly 'the clan/family.' Scholars have tentatively identified it with Lifta, a village northwest of Jerusalem, though the identification remains uncertain. The town appears only in Joshua's list of Benjamite cities.

senses.1: This place name appears in Joshua 18:28 within the list of towns assigned to Benjamin. The Hebrew preserves the definite article, suggesting 'the Eleph' was a known location. Translation evidence shows consistent handling as a place name, with most preserving the Hebrew form. The possible connection to Lifta near Jerusalem would place it in Benjamin's northern hill country territory.

gloss_terse: Urged, pressed insistently; Piel verb describing Delilah's persistent pressure on Samson to reveal his secret
gloss_readable: This verb appears in the account of Delilah wearing down Samson's resistance through relentless verbal pressure. The Piel intensive form emphasizes the persistent, aggressive nature of her urging—not a single request but continuous nagging. In Judges 16:16, it stands parallel to 'she pressed him with her words,' creating a powerful picture of psychological manipulation through constant verbal assault that eventually breaks down Samson's resolve.

senses.1: The verb occurs only in Judges 16:16, describing Delilah's tactics against Samson. The parallel with 'she pressed him with her words' and the result 'his soul was vexed to death' shows the intensity of this verbal harassment. Cross-linguistic evidence ('urgió' in Spanish, 'pressa' in French, 'urged' in English) captures the forceful, insistent nature of her approach. This is psychological warfare through unrelenting pressure.

gloss_terse: With his army, with troops; term of uncertain meaning in Proverbs 30:31, possibly referring to a king with his army
gloss_readable: This difficult word appears in Proverbs 30:31 in a list of things that are stately in their stride. The text is uncertain—some scholars see it as derived from Arabic meaning 'the people/army,' hence 'a king with his army.' Others suggest textual corruption, proposing it should read 'God' instead. The context lists impressive creatures (greyhound, male goat, king) that move with dignity and confidence, so an armed king would fit the theme.

senses.1: Occurring only in Proverbs 30:31, this term has puzzled translators. English renders it 'with his army,' Spanish 'con ejército,' suggesting a king accompanied by troops. The French and German leave it untranslated, indicating uncertainty. If the traditional interpretation is correct, it completes a triad of majestic figures: greyhound, male goat, and a king at the head of his army—all exemplars of confident, stately movement.

gloss_terse: The Elkoshite, gentilicic adjective identifying the prophet Nahum by his hometown Elkosh (location unknown)
gloss_readable: This term identifies Nahum as 'the Elkoshite,' meaning a native or resident of Elkosh. The location of Elkosh remains unknown, though various traditions have placed it in Galilee, Assyria (near Mosul), or elsewhere. Jerome mentioned a Galilean village called Elcesi. The gentilicic form (like 'Bethlehemite' or 'Nazarene') was a common way to identify prophets by their hometown or place of ministry.

senses.1: This adjective appears only in Nahum 1:1 as part of the prophet's identification. Unlike many prophets identified by parentage, Nahum is known by his hometown. The uncertain location of Elkosh has led to various proposals, but the name itself is preserved across translations. This geographic identifier would have helped ancient readers locate Nahum within a specific community, though that knowledge has been lost to us.

gloss_terse: And Eltekon, place name; a town in the hill country of Judah north of Hebron, listed in Joshua 15:59
gloss_readable: Eltekon was one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah in the hill country region. It appears in a group of cities north of Hebron in the Judean highlands. Like many ancient settlements mentioned only in boundary and allotment lists, its exact location is no longer certain. The name is preserved in the biblical record as part of Judah's territorial inheritance.

senses.1: This place name occurs in Joshua 15:59 within the hill country allotment to Judah. The conjunction 'and' connects it to the surrounding list of towns in this geographic cluster. Cross-linguistic translations consistently preserve it as a place name, with Spanish, French, and German maintaining recognizable forms. The town's location in the Judean highlands placed it in the heartland of the tribe's territory.

gloss_terse: Foundations, doorposts, supports; architectural term of uncertain meaning in Isaiah 6:4, possibly thresholds or posts
gloss_readable: This architectural term appears in Isaiah's temple vision where 'the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of the one calling.' The exact meaning is debated—suggestions include foundations, doorposts, or supporting structures of the temple entrance. The Hebrew root may relate to 'mother' in a metaphorical sense of supporting or containing. The image is of the temple's structural elements trembling at the divine voice, emphasizing the power and holiness of God's presence.

senses.1: Found only in Isaiah 6:4 in the prophet's inaugural vision. The shaking of these structures at the seraphim's antiphonal cry demonstrates the overwhelming power of God's holiness. Spanish 'quiciales' (door sockets) suggests pivot points, while the root's possible connection to 'mother/support' indicates foundational or supporting architectural elements. The multilingual uncertainty reflects genuine scholarly debate about this rare architectural term.

gloss_terse: Ammah, place name; a hill near Gibeon where Joab halted pursuit of Abner after the battle (2 Samuel 2:24)
gloss_readable: The hill of Ammah was a landmark near Gibeon where Joab and Abishai halted their pursuit of Abner and his men after the battle at the pool of Gibeon. This geographic marker helped readers locate the endpoint of that day's pursuit. The name may derive from a word meaning 'aqueduct' or 'water channel,' which would be appropriate for a landmark in that region. It appears only in the narrative of the civil war between David's forces and the house of Saul.

senses.1: This toponym occurs in 2 Samuel 2:24 as 'the hill of Ammah' that faces Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. The geographic precision of the narrative uses local landmarks to trace the route of the pursuit. All major translations preserve it as a place name. The battle at Gibeon and subsequent pursuit marked a significant episode in the conflict between the houses of Saul and David.

gloss_terse: Master craftsman, architect, artisan; skilled worker or designer, as Wisdom personified in Proverbs 8:30
gloss_readable: This term describes a skilled artisan or master craftsman with firm, reliable workmanship. In Proverbs 8:30, Wisdom speaks of being at God's side as an 'amon'—interpreted as either 'master craftsman/architect' (participating in creation) or 'nursling/beloved child' (delighting the Creator). The former view sees Wisdom as God's co-worker in creation, the latter as God's cherished companion. Both images emphasize Wisdom's intimate presence with God before creation.

senses.1: In Proverbs 8:30, personified Wisdom declares 'I was beside him as an amon.' The ancient versions and modern interpreters divide between 'master workman' (suggesting Wisdom's role in creation's design) and 'beloved child' (emphasizing intimate relationship). Spanish 'arquitecto' and the traditional 'master craftsman' support the former. This ambiguity enriches the portrait of Wisdom as both agent and object of divine delight.

gloss_terse: The craftsmen, the artisans; either skilled workers or (by alternate reading) the multitude deported from Jerusalem
gloss_readable: This term in Jeremiah 52:15 refers to either craftsmen/artisans or possibly 'the multitude' (if reading it as equivalent to 'hamon'). In the context of Nebuchadnezzar's deportation of Jerusalem, it describes a group taken into exile. If 'craftsmen,' it indicates the Babylonians specifically targeted skilled workers—smiths, builders, artisans—whose expertise would benefit the empire. If 'multitude,' it refers more generally to masses of people. The ambiguity reflects textual uncertainty.

senses.1: Jeremiah 52:15 lists 'the rest of the craftsmen' among those deported to Babylon. Spanish 'la multitud' suggests the alternate reading where this equals 'hamon' (multitude). The strategic deportation of skilled workers was standard Babylonian policy—removing both potential rebel leadership and technical expertise. Whether craftsmen specifically or the populace generally, this group represents the draining of Jerusalem's human resources after the city's fall in 586 BC.

gloss_terse: Ami, personal name; head of a family of temple servants who returned from exile (Ezra 2:57, called Amon in Nehemiah 7:59)
gloss_readable: Ami was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. The parallel passage in Nehemiah 7:59 calls him Amon, showing the kind of minor textual variation common in biblical genealogies. The Nethinim were temple workers who assisted the Levites in various duties. This family maintained their identity and service role through the exile and into the restoration period.

senses.1: This name appears in Ezra 2:57 among the returning temple servants. The variant 'Amon' in Nehemiah 7:59 demonstrates typical scribal variation in proper names. These families of temple servants preserved their ancestral identity through generations of exile, returning to resume their hereditary roles in temple service. The name itself means 'my people' or possibly 'trustworthy,' fitting for one whose descendants served faithfully.

gloss_terse: Languishing, feeble, faint; adjective describing physical weakness or exhaustion from distress
gloss_readable: This adjective describes physical languishing or feebleness, often from grief or distress. In Psalm 6:2, the psalmist cries out in physical and emotional anguish: 'I am languishing.' The term conveys the bodily effects of deep trouble—weakness, exhaustion, wasting away. It stands parallel to 'my bones are troubled,' showing how emotional and spiritual distress manifests in physical debility. This vocabulary of illness and weakness is common in lament psalms.

senses.1: Found in Psalm 6:2 where the psalmist pleads for divine mercy while describing his languishing condition. Spanish 'desfallecido' (failing, fainting) and English 'languishing' capture the sense of wasting weakness. The parallel 'my bones are troubled' intensifies the image of comprehensive distress affecting the whole person. Lament psalms frequently use physical vocabulary to express spiritual and emotional anguish, making the suffering tangible and urgent.

gloss_terse: The feeble, the weak; plural adjective describing powerless or vulnerable people, used mockingly in Nehemiah 4:2
gloss_readable: This term describes people who are feeble, weak, or powerless. In Nehemiah 4:2, enemies of the rebuilding project mockingly ask, 'What are these feeble Jews doing?' The insult targets the builders' perceived weakness and inability to complete the massive task of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls. The question drips with contempt—how can this weak, dispirited remnant possibly accomplish such a work? Nehemiah's response is to pray and continue building.

senses.1: Nehemiah 4:2 (Hebrew v. 2) records Sanballat's mocking question about 'these feeble Jews' attempting to rebuild the walls. Spanish 'débiles' (weak) and the LXX tradition capture the contemptuous tone. The taunt assumes the returned exiles lack the strength, resources, and capacity to complete such an ambitious construction project. This epithet 'feeble' becomes part of the opposition's psychological warfare against the rebuilders, which Nehemiah counters with prayer and persistent work.

gloss_terse: Amam, place name; a town in the southern district of Judah, listed in Joshua 15:26
gloss_readable: Amam was a town in the Negev region assigned to Judah's tribal territory. It appears in the list of cities in Judah's southern district, the arid zone extending toward Edom. Like many settlements in this list, its precise location is no longer known. The Septuagint preserves variant readings, showing the textual uncertainty common with place names in this region. These southern towns marked Judah's frontier in the wilderness.

senses.1: This toponym occurs in Joshua 15:26 within the catalog of Judah's southernmost towns. The Septuagint shows textual variation (some manuscripts read 'Amam,' others 'Shen'), typical for place names in remote areas. These Negev settlements represented Judah's territorial claims in the harsh southern frontier, though many may have been seasonal or marginal sites. The preservation of the name in the biblical record maintains the memory of Judah's full territorial extent.

gloss_terse: You turn to the right; imperfect verb describing turning or veering to the right side, used figuratively in Isaiah 30:21
gloss_readable: This verb describes turning or going to the right. In Isaiah 30:21, it appears in a promise about divine guidance: when God's people start to turn aside either to the right or left from the proper path, they will hear a voice behind them saying 'This is the way, walk in it.' The right and left represent deviations in either direction from the straight path of obedience. The image is of God as a shepherd or guide correcting wayward movement.

senses.1: Isaiah 30:21 uses this verb in parallel with 'turn to the left' to describe any deviation from the right path. The context promises that after judgment, God's people will receive clear guidance—a voice directing them back to the true way whenever they begin to stray. The bilateral image (right or left) covers all possible deviations. This echoes Deuteronomic language about not turning aside from God's commandments to the right or left.

gloss_terse: Craftsman, master workman, artisan; skilled worker, particularly one who creates fine or artistic work
gloss_readable: This term designates a skilled craftsman or artisan, particularly one whose work shows artistic mastery. In Song of Solomon 7:1, it describes 'the work of a craftsman's hands' in admiring the beloved's beauty. The comparison to skilled artisanship elevates the natural beauty being described, suggesting divine or human craft at the highest level. The term appears in later Hebrew and Aramaic contexts for master workers in various crafts.

senses.1: In Song of Solomon 7:1 (Hebrew 7:2), the lover praises the beloved's form as 'the work of a craftsman's hands.' Spanish 'artesano' and French 'artisan' capture the sense of skilled artistic work. The comparison treats human beauty as comparable to the finest artistic creation, whether divine or human craftsmanship. This aesthetic appreciation through artistic metaphor is characteristic of the Song's elevated poetic style.

gloss_terse: Truth, faithfulness, reliability; noun emphasizing firm trustworthiness, used in construct with 'faithfulness' (Isaiah 25:1)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes firm faithfulness or truth. In Isaiah 25:1, it appears in an emphatic construct phrase: 'faithfulness and truth' or 'perfect faithfulness' (literally 'faithfulness, faithfulness'—using two synonymous words for emphasis). The prophet praises God for carrying out ancient plans with complete reliability. This doubled expression ('emunah' and 'omen') intensifies the assertion of God's absolute trustworthiness in fulfilling His purposes through history.

senses.1: Found only in Isaiah 25:1 in the phrase 'faithfulness and truth' (or 'perfect faithfulness'). Spanish 'verdad' (truth) reflects one aspect of the semantic range. The construct pairing of two near-synonyms creates emphatic assertion—God's plans are characterized by absolute, unwavering faithfulness. This praise follows the prophecy of judgment on the nations, celebrating God's reliability in executing His stated purposes across generations.

gloss_terse: In guardianship, in foster care; noun describing the act of raising or caring for someone, used of Esther's upbringing
gloss_readable: This term refers to the act of bringing up, fostering, or guardianship. In Esther 2:20, it describes Esther continuing to follow Mordecai's instructions just as she had during her 'upbringing' or 'guardianship' under him. The word emphasizes the nurturing care and guidance Mordecai provided for his orphaned cousin. Even after becoming queen, Esther maintained the obedience and trust established during her years under Mordecai's foster care.

senses.1: Esther 2:20 uses this term for the period when Mordecai raised Esther after she was orphaned. Spanish 'crianza' (upbringing/rearing) captures the nurturing aspect. The text emphasizes continuity—Esther's obedience to Mordecai persists even in her new royal status, because it was established during her formative years under his guardianship. This foster care relationship becomes crucial to the story's plot as Mordecai continues to guide Esther's actions.

gloss_terse: The doorposts, the jambs; architectural term for the posts or supports of a doorway, mentioned in 2 Kings 18:16
gloss_readable: This term refers to doorposts or supporting pillars of doorways. In 2 Kings 18:16, it describes the posts of the temple doors that King Hezekiah had overlaid with gold, which he then stripped off to pay tribute to the Assyrian king Sennacherib. This desperate act of despoiling even the sacred temple doors shows the severity of the crisis. The doorposts may have been structural supports or decorative elements framing the temple entrances.

senses.1: Second Kings 18:16 records Hezekiah stripping gold from 'the doorposts' of the temple to pay Assyrian tribute. The Hebrew root connects to 'those brought up' or 'supported,' suggesting pillars or posts. Spanish 'jambas' (jambs/doorposts) identifies the structural elements framing doorways. The detail that these had been covered in gold shows both the temple's former glory and the severity of Hezekiah's emergency—he removed precious metal even from the sacred structure itself.

gloss_terse: Strength, might, fortitude; noun describing inner strength or power that increases through righteousness
gloss_readable: This noun denotes strength, might, or fortitude—particularly inner moral or physical strength. In Job 17:9, it appears in the statement that 'the clean of hands will increase in strength.' This affirms that moral purity leads to growing strength rather than weakness. Against the common assumption that wickedness brings power and righteousness leads to vulnerability, Job asserts that integrity actually strengthens a person. The righteous grow stronger through their trials.

senses.1: Job 17:9 uses this term in a proverbial statement: 'the one who has clean hands will add strength.' Spanish 'fuerza' (strength/force) captures the basic sense. Job affirms a moral principle—righteousness produces increasing strength, not weakness. This counterintuitive claim challenges the assumption that ethical compromise is necessary for power. Instead, integrity itself becomes a source of fortification, with the morally pure person growing stronger over time.

gloss_terse: Strength, might; noun used in Zechariah 12:5 in a difficult phrase about finding strength in inhabitants of Jerusalem
gloss_readable: This term denotes strength or might. It appears in Zechariah 12:5 in a notoriously difficult phrase where the leaders of Judah recognize strength in Jerusalem's inhabitants. The Hebrew is uncertain—some interpret it as 'the inhabitants of Jerusalem are my strength,' others suggest textual emendation. The context describes divine strengthening of Judah's leaders, so the sense involves finding courage or military capacity through recognition of Jerusalem's divinely-protected inhabitants.

senses.1: Zechariah 12:5 contains this term in a textually and interpretively difficult verse. Spanish 'Fuerza' (strength) represents one reading, though the exact construction remains debated. The Septuagint and other versions show variation. The general sense is that Judah's leaders find strength or confidence in Jerusalem's inhabitants (who themselves are strengthened by God). This mutual encouragement forms part of the prophecy about Judah's deliverance and Jerusalem's protection.

gloss_terse: His word, His utterance; construct noun with pronominal suffix referring to God's declared word or command
gloss_readable: This term refers to God's word, utterance, or spoken decree. In Lamentations 2:17, it appears in the phrase 'His word which He commanded'—referring to the prophetic warnings and covenant curses God had declared long beforehand. The verse asserts that the destruction of Jerusalem was not arbitrary but the fulfillment of God's explicitly stated word. The term emphasizes the spoken, declared nature of God's purposes, now being carried out in judgment.

senses.1: Lamentations 2:17 uses this construct form ('His word') to reference the prophetic warnings and covenant curses God had spoken through Moses and the prophets. The destruction of Jerusalem fulfills 'His word which He commanded of old.' This theological interpretation of the catastrophe sees it not as random disaster but as the execution of long-declared divine judgment. The term stresses the verbal, declarative nature of God's purposes, now being implemented in history.

gloss_terse: And dreadful, and terrible; Aramaic adjective describing something inspiring fear or awe, used of the fourth beast in Daniel
gloss_readable: This Aramaic adjective means dreadful, terrible, or awe-inspiring. In Daniel 7:7, it describes the fourth beast in Daniel's vision as 'terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong.' The adjective emphasizes the fear-inspiring nature of this beast, which represents a future empire of unprecedented brutality and power. The accumulation of terms (terrifying, dreadful, strong, different) creates an image of something uniquely fearsome in the succession of kingdoms.

senses.1: Daniel 7:7 applies this adjective to the fourth beast in the vision of successive empires. Spanish 'espantosa' (frightening) and French 'terrible' convey the sense of inspiring terror or dread. The beast is characterized by multiple fear-inducing qualities—it's not just strong but dreadful, with great iron teeth. This apocalyptic imagery presents a future power that surpasses previous kingdoms in its capacity to inspire fear and inflict destruction.

gloss_terse: We (ketiv variant); first person plural pronoun variant spelling in Jeremiah 42:6, standard spelling is 'anachnu'
gloss_readable: This represents the ketiv (written) form of the first person plural pronoun 'we' in Jeremiah 42:6, where the standard spelling is 'anachnu.' Such orthographic variants are common in Hebrew manuscripts—the written form and the traditional reading sometimes differ slightly. Both forms mean the same thing: 'we.' In this passage, the people declare their intention to obey the Lord's word whether it is pleasant or difficult: 'We will obey the voice of the Lord our God.'

senses.1: This orthographic variant appears in Jeremiah 42:6 where the remnant pledges obedience to God's word. The ketiv/qere note indicates a variant spelling of the common pronoun 'we.' All translations naturally render it as 'we' or the vernacular equivalent. The variant spelling doesn't affect meaning but shows the text-critical reality of minor orthographic differences in Hebrew manuscripts. The content—the people's solemn vow to obey—matters more than the spelling variation.

gloss_terse: They are (feminine); Aramaic third person feminine plural pronoun in Daniel 7:17, ketiv reading 'innun'
gloss_readable: This Aramaic pronoun represents the feminine plural 'they' in Daniel 7:17. The text has a ketiv/qere variation—the written form is 'innun' (masculine), but the traditional reading is 'innin' (feminine), agreeing with the feminine noun 'beasts.' The angel explains Daniel's vision: 'These great beasts, which are four, are four kings who will arise from the earth.' The pronoun connects the symbolic beasts to their interpretation as earthly kingdoms.

senses.1: In Daniel 7:17, this feminine pronoun refers back to the four great beasts of Daniel's vision. The qere reading 'innin' (feminine) agrees grammatically with 'beasts,' while the ketiv 'innun' is masculine. All translations render it naturally as 'they' in context: the four beasts represent four kings/kingdoms. The gender agreement issue is minor—the point is the symbolic interpretation linking the terrifying vision to historical political powers.

gloss_terse: And Anaharath, place name; a town in the territory of Issachar, listed in Joshua 19:19
gloss_readable: Anaharath was a town allotted to the tribe of Issachar in the division of the land. It appears in the boundary description of Issachar's territory in the Jezreel Valley region. The exact location is uncertain, though some scholars have proposed sites in the valley area. Like many towns in these allotment lists, the name is preserved in Scripture though the site itself can no longer be identified with certainty.

senses.1: This toponym occurs in Joshua 19:19 among the towns of Issachar's inheritance. The conjunction 'and' links it to the surrounding list of territorial markers. Issachar's allotment included fertile valley land in the Jezreel and surrounding areas. Translations consistently preserve it as a place name, with minor variations in transliteration. The preservation of these geographic markers maintains the biblical record of tribal territorial assignments.

gloss_terse: And Aniam, personal name; a descendant of Manasseh mentioned in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:19
gloss_readable: Aniam was a member of the tribe of Manasseh, appearing in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles. The name is preserved in the tribal lineage but without additional narrative information. Like many names in Chronicles' genealogies, it maintains the memory of clan heads or family representatives within Manasseh's complex tribal structure. The name's etymology is uncertain, though it may contain a theophoric element.

senses.1: This personal name appears in 1 Chronicles 7:19 within Manasseh's genealogy. The name occurs only once, with no other information about the individual. Translations preserve the Hebrew form with minor variations in transliteration. These genealogical lists served to maintain tribal identity and land claims, recording family heads whose descendants formed clans within the larger tribe. The preservation of the name honors the person's place in Manasseh's lineage.

gloss_terse: Compelling, forcing; participle describing one who forces or constrains others, negated in Esther 1:8 to mean 'no compulsion'
gloss_readable: This verb means to compel, constrain, or force someone to act against their will. In Esther 1:8, it appears in the negative: 'there was no compulsion' at King Ahasuerus's banquet—guests could drink as much or as little as they wished. The term indicates coercion or forcing someone into action. The absence of such compulsion at the royal feast shows unusual royal generosity and respect for guests' preferences, contrary to typical ancient Near Eastern royal banquet protocol.

senses.1: Esther 1:8 uses this participle negatively to indicate drinking at the royal banquet was voluntary: 'there was no one compelling.' Spanish 'obligación' (obligation/compulsion) captures the sense. The king commanded that guests be allowed to drink according to their own wish, without forced conformity to royal drinking customs. This detail characterizes Ahasuerus's banquet as remarkably permissive, with guests free from the usual social compulsion to match the king's consumption.

gloss_terse: Is difficult; Aramaic participle describing something oppressing or troubling someone, used in Daniel 4:9
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb means to oppress, trouble, or be difficult. In Daniel 4:9 (Aramaic 4:6), King Nebuchadnezzar tells Daniel that 'no mystery is difficult for you'—meaning Daniel has the ability to interpret even the most challenging dreams or visions. The term indicates something pressing, burdensome, or beyond normal capacity to solve. The king's confidence in Daniel reflects the previous successful interpretation and Daniel's proven connection to divine wisdom.

senses.1: Daniel 4:9 (Aramaic v. 6) contains Nebuchadnezzar's statement that no secret is 'difficult' or 'too hard' for Daniel. Spanish 'te es difícil' (is difficult for you) renders the sense clearly. The king has witnessed Daniel's interpretive gift and knows that mysteries impenetrable to others are accessible to Daniel through divine revelation. This sets up the dream interpretation that follows, where Daniel must deliver troubling news to the king.

gloss_terse: And the gecko; unclean reptile listed in Leviticus 11:30, possibly a lizard species or ferret (identification uncertain)
gloss_readable: This term identifies an unclean animal in the Levitical purity laws, traditionally understood as a type of lizard (gecko) or possibly a shrew-mouse. It appears in the list of swarming creatures that are ritually unclean and forbidden as food. The exact species identification is uncertain—ancient and modern interpreters have proposed various small reptiles or rodents. What matters for the law is its classification among the prohibited creatures.

senses.1: Leviticus 11:30 lists this creature among unclean swarming things. English and French 'gecko,' Spanish 'erizo' (hedgehog), and German 'gecko' show the uncertainty of identification. The term appears only here in the unclean animal catalog. Whether a specific lizard species, shrew, or other small creature, it belonged to the category of swarming animals that made a person ritually unclean through contact. The taxonomy matters less than the ritual boundary it marked.

gloss_terse: You (masculine plural); Aramaic second person plural pronoun addressing multiple male individuals
gloss_readable: This Aramaic pronoun is the standard second person masculine plural 'you' (equivalent to Hebrew 'attem'). In Daniel 2:8, King Nebuchadnezzar uses it to address his counselors: 'I know that you are trying to gain time.' The pronoun marks direct address to a group of men. It's the ordinary plural 'you' in Aramaic, used throughout Daniel's Aramaic chapters for addressing groups of officials, counselors, or others.

senses.1: Daniel 2:8 contains this pronoun in Nebuchadnezzar's accusation against his advisors. All translations render it naturally with the plural 'you' or language-specific equivalents (Spanish 'vosotros,' French 'vous,' German 'ihr'). The king suspects his counselors are stalling, trying to buy time because they cannot actually interpret dreams. This common pronoun carries no special significance beyond its grammatical function of marking plural address.

gloss_terse: A jar of, flask of; construct noun for a container or vessel, used in 2 Kings 4:2 for a jar of oil
gloss_readable: This term designates a jar, flask, or container, particularly for holding oil or other liquids. In 2 Kings 4:2, the widow tells Elisha that all she has in her house is 'a jar of oil.' The form is unusual and the text may be uncertain, but the meaning is clear—a vessel containing oil. This small amount of oil becomes the seed for Elisha's miracle of multiplying oil to pay the widow's debts and save her sons from slavery.

senses.1: Second Kings 4:2 uses this construct form for the widow's 'jar of oil.' Spanish 'vasija de' (vessel of) and English 'jar of' convey the basic sense of a container. Though the Hebrew form is textually uncertain (some suggest emendations), the meaning is contextually clear—a small vessel containing oil, which becomes the instrument of miraculous provision. The widow's honest assessment of her poverty makes the subsequent abundance more striking.

gloss_terse: Asnah, personal name; head of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile in Ezra 2:50
gloss_readable: Asnah was the ancestral head of a family of Nethinim (temple servants) who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The name possibly derives from Aramaic meaning 'thorn-bush.' Interestingly, this name appears in Ezra's list but is omitted in the parallel passage in Nehemiah 7:52, showing the textual variation between these two registers of returnees. The family maintained its identity through exile and resumed temple service in the restoration.

senses.1: This personal name occurs in Ezra 2:50 among families of temple servants returning from Babylon. The omission from Nehemiah's parallel list shows typical variation in genealogical records. The proposed etymology from Aramaic 'thorn-bush' is uncertain but plausible. These Nethinim families served practical roles in temple operations, and the preservation of their names honors their faithful service across the generations of exile and return.

gloss_terse: Osnappar (Ashurbanipal), proper name; the Assyrian king who deported peoples to Samaria (Ezra 4:10), likely Ashurbanipal (668-626 BC)
gloss_readable: Osnappar is identified as the Assyrian king who transported foreign populations to Samaria, part of Assyria's policy of mixing conquered peoples to prevent rebellion. Most scholars identify him with Ashurbanipal (Akkadian: Ashur-bani-apli), who reigned 668–626 BC. The Hebrew form preserves an abbreviated version of the Assyrian name. This deportation policy explains the mixed population of Samaria in the post-exilic period and the Samaritans' claim to participate in rebuilding the temple.

senses.1: Ezra 4:10 references 'the great and noble Osnappar' who deported peoples to Samaria. The identification with Ashurbanipal is well-established—the Hebrew represents a shortened form of the Assyrian king's name. The Septuagint variant 'Salmanasar' (Shalmaneser) reflects confusion between Assyrian kings. Ashurbanipal's deportation policy created the mixed population later called Samaritans, whose desire to join the temple rebuilding is rejected by the returned exiles, creating ongoing conflict.

gloss_terse: A gathering, a collecting; verbal noun describing the act of gathering prisoners or captives together
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the act of gathering, collecting, or assembling. In Isaiah 24:22, it appears in a difficult phrase describing prisoners being 'gathered with a gathering into the pit.' The expression may be emphatic ('truly gathered') or describe the manner of their collection. The context is eschatological judgment where hostile powers are imprisoned, awaiting final judgment. The verbal noun emphasizes the action of assembling or bringing together these captive forces.

senses.1: Isaiah 24:22 contains this term in the phrase describing how enemies are 'gathered (with a gathering) as prisoners unto the pit.' Spanish 'reunión de' (gathering of) captures the nominal sense. The construction may be emphatic or descriptive—they are assembled collectively, en masse, into confinement. This apocalyptic imagery depicts divine judgment comprehensively imprisoning hostile powers, who remain confined until their final visitation. The noun stresses the totality of their assembly.

gloss_terse: Collections, assemblies; plural noun in Ecclesiastes 12:11, possibly referring to collected sayings or assemblies of wise teachers
gloss_readable: This term refers to collections or assemblies. In Ecclesiastes 12:11, it appears in the phrase 'masters of assemblies' or 'masters of collections,' in a passage describing wise sayings as nails firmly fixed. The meaning is debated: either (1) members of learned assemblies—wise teachers gathered in scholarly communities, or (2) the wise sayings themselves, called 'masters of collections' because they are well-organized, collected teachings. Both views emphasize the authoritative, organized nature of wisdom.

senses.1: Ecclesiastes 12:11 uses this term in a famously difficult phrase comparing wise words to firmly driven nails, given by 'masters of assemblies/collections.' Post-biblical Hebrew uses related terms for assemblies or gatherings. The phrase might indicate wise teachers as members of learned communities, or refer to the collected, systematized nature of their teachings. Either way, it points to wisdom's organized, established, authoritative character—not random observations but collected, refined truth.

gloss_terse: And the rabble, and the mixed multitude; noun describing a mixed crowd or disorderly mob, used of camp followers at the Exodus
gloss_readable: This term refers to a mixed rabble or collection of people, specifically the non-Israelite camp followers who accompanied Israel out of Egypt. In Numbers 11:4, 'the rabble' among them had strong cravings for meat and influenced the Israelites to complain against the manna. This mixed multitude—probably Egyptians and others who joined the Exodus—became a source of discontent and temptation. They exemplify how outside influences can corrupt community faithfulness.

senses.1: Numbers 11:4 identifies 'the rabble' (asafsuf) among the Israelites as instigators of the craving for meat, sparking widespread complaint. Spanish 'chusma' (rabble/mob) captures the pejorative tone. These mixed multitude camp followers, who attached themselves to Israel during the Exodus, lacked the covenant relationship and became agents of discontent. Their craving infected Israel, leading to the quail judgment. The term suggests a disorganized, unreliable collection of hangers-on rather than covenant people.

gloss_terse: Aspatha, personal name; the third son of Haman listed among those killed by the Jews in Esther 9:7
gloss_readable: Aspatha was the third son of Haman the Agagite, killed along with his nine brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies. The name is Persian, possibly meaning 'given by the horse' (sacred) according to Persian etymology. The listing of all ten sons by name in Esther 9 emphasizes the complete reversal of Haman's planned destruction of the Jews—his own family line is cut off instead. Their death represents the failure of Amalekite enmity against Israel.

senses.1: Esther 9:7 lists Aspatha third among Haman's ten sons executed on the day of Jewish self-defense. The preservation of all ten Persian names (unusual in Hebrew Scripture) emphasizes the completeness of the reversal—the genocidal plotter's own line is exterminated. The probable Persian etymology ('given by the sacred horse') shows authentic Persian nomenclature. The sons' death fulfills the principle that those who plot Israel's destruction bring destruction on their own house.
